speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The principles and provisions of the Act underpin the National Environment Agency’s (NEA’s) work on public cleanliness and waste management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We cannot take for granted our clean and green environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The environmental services (ES) industry, which includes cleaning and waste management companies, face real challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Many of the jobs are shunned by Singaporeans, who perceive them as dirty, demanding or dangerous.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The industry is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For instance, a large proportion of jobs in the waste collection industry are filled by foreign workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The ES ITM will drive innovation and wider technology adoption, upskill workers to take on better jobs, improve productivity and capture value overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These will improve working conditions and equip workers with relevant skills to thrive in the future economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The ES ITM will not take away the jobs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As it is, there are simply not enough Singaporeans who want to join the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We need to grow a vibrant ES sector which can compete with the best in the world and provide more higher value-added jobs which can attract Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is the only way for us to reduce our reliance on foreign labour in the long run.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The measures which I will speak about will help address the challenges the ES industry faces, and ensure that Singapore continues to be a clean, green and liveable city for generations to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Government has made a concerted push to expand the use of pneumatic waste conveyance systems (PWCS) in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: PWCS is a tried and tested technology that uses air pressure to convey waste through sealed pipes from throw-points to a bin centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Earlier this year, I visited Hammarby Sjöstad, a sustainable community in Stockholm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Over there, they first implemented a PWCS more than three decades ago, in 1982, to collect waste from 3,000 apartments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Over the years, they have added another two PWCS in the area to serve 5,000 more apartments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This shift to PWCS is akin to Singapore’s transition from night soil buckets to sewerage pipes in our early years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: It replaces the need for cleaners to manually collect waste from individual apartment blocks and bring it to a bin centre, a common sight in many condominiums and Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will transform waste collection and allow us to improve the standards of cleanliness and public health, even with a shrinking workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Disamenities to residents, such as pests and odour, are reduced as the entire system is enclosed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Developments and their cleaning contractors will save on manpower needed to transfer waste and clean spillages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These jobs will be replaced by higher value-added jobs, such as maintenance technicians and project engineers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These are jobs which we envision creating for Singaporeans under ES ITM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We have been taking steady steps towards this vision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will add to the more than 140 private residential and commercial developments which have already done so on their own accord.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: We will introduce a new Part IIIA to the Act to enable PWCS to be deployed at the district level, beyond individual developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As Minister for National Development Mr Lawrence Wong announced at last year’s Committee of Supply, this is part of plans to transform Kampong Bugis into a people-centric and car-lite precinct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Legislation is necessary as private developers are unlikely to, on their own, come together to embark on a district-level system, thus missing out on the benefits from scale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Moreover, as DPWCS is best implemented on a greenfield site where the sale or redevelopment of individual plots are likely to take place at different times, it would otherwise be very difficult to coordinate its implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: By implementing PWCS at the district level, we can reap more economies of scale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For example, instead of having bin centres in each development, the district can share a central bin centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Refuse truck traffic within the district will also be reduced, as refuse will only be collected from one bin centre, which can be located away from residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: HDB and JTC are already implementing the PWCS at the district level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: In 2015, HDB retrofitted 38 blocks in Yuhua estate under its Greenprint programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Feedback from residents indicated that many were satisfied with the PWCS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For example, there was a reduction in odour and pests and an improvement in estate cleanliness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The lessons from Yuhua will be incorporated into the district-level PWCS in new estates, including Tampines North and Punggol.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: JTC is also exploring PWCS at the district level in their new business parks, such as the Punggol Digital District.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Where needed, section 31H will allow the Minister to modify or revoke declarations of the DPWCS area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Before these powers are exercised, the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) and NEA will provide advance notice to affected stakeholders in the Gazette under section 31I.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: An avenue for written representation to the Minister is also provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This minimises disruptions to residents served by the DPWCS by ensuring that the company taking on the project will be properly regulated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Standard will cover basic requirements for the construction and installation of the network and guidelines on maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: For example, the licensee can conduct excavation works, provided the necessary approvals from authorities are obtained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These rights are similar to those provided to gas transporter licensees under the Gas Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will be referring to this handout as I explain the next section which talks about three key components in the DPWCS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This "refuse pipeline network", indicated in brown on the handout, refers to the main DPWCS network which will be shared across the district.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will be owned and maintained by NEA or the DPWCS licensee.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Individual premises would own their internal PWCS pipes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is marked in blue on the handout and termed "related internal assets".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will be the responsibility of the premises owners to maintain and operate the internal PWCS pipes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The connection to the refuse pipeline network will be demarcated by a “connection point” – the triangle in the handout.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will be considered part of the refuse pipeline network.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Taking Kampong Bugis as an example, NEA will collect the connection charge from the Master Developer that is appointed to plan and develop the site.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When a particular development, for example, a condominium, has been built at Kampong Bugis, the tariffs will be collected by the DPWCS licensee from either the developer or the Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) when it is formed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also make related amendments to sections 16(2) and 39(1) of the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act (BMSMA), so that connection charges and tariffs can be paid from the maintenance fund.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will also allow contributions from subsidiary proprietors to be raised for these payments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Sections 31P to 31R will make it an offence to conduct works that break or would otherwise affect the ground without first ascertaining the location of refuse pipes in the DPWCS area.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will also be an offence to damage the DPWCS or affect its operations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similar provisions are found in the District Cooling Act, Gas Act and Public Utilities Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is to minimise inconvenience and potential public health risks to residents in the district.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Section 31T will protect the DPWCS assets from distress or being liable to be taken in execution under Court processes, in cases where the DPWCS owner faces bankruptcy or insolvency.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under certain circumstances, the new section 31V will allow NEA to take over management of the DPWCS under a special administration order to ensure that the DPWCS will continue to function.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through implementing PWCS, we will upgrade the waste collection industry and improve the environment for everyone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even as we harness technology to enhance our ES, we must not forget the people behind them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A skilled workforce will be crucial for sustaining productivity growth as our labour situation tightens.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2014, we introduced the mandatory Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the cleaning sector, to upgrade the skills and wages of our resident cleaners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This was done to boost the income levels of cleaners sustainably and improve productivity and standards in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many businesses were paying cleaners above the minimum PWM wage level to attract capable staff.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Sectoral productivity also improved as companies adopted technology to save manhours and improve work conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2016, the Tripartite Cluster for Cleaners (TCC) proposed a suite of recommendations to build on this momentum.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These included yearly wage adjustments between 2017 to 2022 to sustain wage growth, and an annual PWM Bonus to be paid from 2020, to encourage cleaners to stay on their jobs and raise their incomes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government had given its full support to the TCC's recommendations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This Bill reaffirms that support by introducing the PWM Bonus as a licensing requirement for cleaning businesses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through amendments to sections 80G and 80H of the Act, it will become mandatory for every licensed cleaning business to provide for the payment of a PWM Bonus to its eligible resident cleaners, regardless of the worker's performance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Cleaning businesses which do not comply will face financial penalties or risk losing their licence, similar to how other PWM-related offences are dealt with.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Commissioner for Labour (CoL) will, based on the TCC’s recommendations, specify in an order the minimum amount, frequency of payment, and eligible class of cleaners for the PWM Bonus.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, the minimum quantum recommended by TCC is two weeks of the basic monthly wage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Coupled with the scheduled annual wage increments, cleaners receiving PWM basic wages today could see their salaries increase by up to 7% each year from now till 2020, when the PWM Bonus is mandated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More details will be released in due course.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But our efforts alone will not be enough; employers and service buyers must also act responsibly and reward staff fairly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Only by working together can we realise our vision of a skilled and productive cleaning workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Section 98 will be amended for greater efficiency in serving documents required or authorised under the Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, regulatory documents, such as summonses, must be served by hand to only the secretary of an errant company.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Additionally, if the document is not intended for proceedings in Court, it can now be served by fax.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many other Acts, like the Environmental Protection and Management Act, similarly provide for such methods of service.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will deter belligerent offenders from hampering NEA's enforcement efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A similar provision can be found in the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Taken together, these changes will minimise abortive enforcement work and enable NEA to optimise limited resources.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Serious public health implications may arise from the unlicensed operation of such facilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have explained how we will leverage technology to manage our waste efficiently through DPWCS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have also shared how we will help our cleaners upskill, upgrade and earn higher wages through our tripartite efforts, even as we automate many of the tasks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have made progress over the years, but more must be done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Businesses must proactively develop the skillsets of their workers in order to realise the benefits of a productive and committed workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Workers should also be nimble, adaptable and open to learning new skills.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to support our stakeholders to transform the ES industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The graciousness of a society can be measured by how it treats the less fortunate in its midst.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It would be a hollow victory for us to achieve success as a nation if we, as a society, do nothing to help the less fortunate when we have the means to do so.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For the longest time, the basic salaries earned by our resident cleaners stagnated and remained low.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coupled with the lack of bonus payouts, our local cleaners had little left for savings after spending on local necessities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other than statutory employment benefits, most employers also do not provide them with added welfare benefits or incentives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Overall, our cleaners had little job security and would have difficulty to save for a rainy day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The plight of our resident cleaners has not gone unnoticed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through the efforts of the TCC, things have been improving for them, with concrete steps being taken to improve their lot.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coupled with the Workfare Income Supplement scheme, many resident cleaners today are seeing an increase in their take-home pay and Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2017, the cleaning industry, as part of the ES sector, had also developed an ITM that would provide a blueprint to transform the industry, with workers playing an integral role.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A key strategy identified in the ITM was the need to sustain a strong and productive cleaning workforce by putting in place structures and processes to ensure workers in ES are Ready for new jobs, Relevant with new skills and Resilient to new ways of working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Efforts to help the vulnerable workers in the cleaning industry are still a work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, we are again presented with an opportunity to make a difference to the lives of this vulnerable group of workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The passing of the amendments in this Bill will be another historic and landmark change for our resident cleaners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It will put an end to the common work grievance of many resident cleaners of not being paid bonuses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This amendment recognises that part of the industry’s transformation will be underpinned by productive and well-skilled workers, and this compulsory PWM Bonus will be a great boost to sustain a strong and highly motivated cleaning workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am in full support of the Bill which will make the PWM Bonus a requirement and condition of NEA’s licensing condition regime.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened that the PWM Bonus is not contingent on the workers’ performance and must be paid so long as the resident cleaner meets the criteria set out by TCC.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will ensure our resident cleaners will have a day or two every year for them to look forward to a bonus payout.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our hope that the PWM Bonus will serve as a motivational tool to encourage workers to stay longer with the same employer, as well as incentivise employers to invest in training their cleaners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As cleaners scale the PWM wage ladder, the rising wages will be accompanied by higher productivity and growth for the industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, full restitution must still be made to the affected cleaners if the employers fail to pay them the bonus.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To provide greater clarity on the technicalities of the PWM Bonus payment, the TCC secretariat will issue an addendum report and a list of frequently asked questions later this year.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Efforts to improve the lives of our cleaners cannot be the sole responsibility of the industry stakeholders represented by TCC.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we may have heard of the common saying, "It takes a village to raise a child", I would say it takes the whole society to play our part to help our cleaners have better lives, for them and their families.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Improving the wages and skillsets of our cleaners are just the tip of the iceberg of what we can do to help them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the PWM and payment of PWM Bonus would be made mandatory, unfortunately, TCC cannot mandate service buyers to shoulder the same responsibility in their procurement of cleaning services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To all service buyers, my message is simple.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You can buy services, but you cannot outsource your responsibilities!

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my engagement with many cleaning companies, one common feedback is that the practice of cheap sourcing is still rampant amongst service buyers, both in the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The 1,300 cleaning companies will then respond by lowering their tender prices, with possibly putting in suicide bids to win contracts, much to the detriment of the whole cleaning industry in the long run.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With rising overheads and business cost, the only way to remain afloat is to pay the workers at the minimum PWM wages and not to give any other welfare benefits.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can lead to a vicious cycle where the level of service is compromised when service providers cut corners to remain in business and the workers would have low morale.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With very low margins, there is little incentive for cleaning companies to invest in technology or training.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to urge all service buyers, whether they are commercial, industrial building owners, private condominiums or Government agencies, to work with their potential service providers to ensure the tender prices commensurate with the level of the service expected, the investment in technology and training needed and, at the same time, without compromising the welfare of the cleaners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This requires service buyers to truly best source beyond paying lip service.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service buyers can discourage cheap sourcing by not awarding to the lowest bidder.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will send a clear signal to industry that it is quality and not price that matters.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cleaning companies must also do the right thing to ensure the long-term sustainability of the industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Walk away if winning the contract entails you cutting corners for you to survive.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For the rest of us, we can also do our part to make the work of our vulnerable, elderly cleaners easier by not littering, returning our trays, exercising our civic consciousness in using public amenities, and many others.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We live and breathe in the same space and it is our collective responsibility to create a pleasant environment for ourselves and our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The manpower challenges faced by the ES industry is real as we face an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This system will rely on air pressure to convey waste via pipes to a bin centre, eliminating the need to manually haul refuse.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It will also eliminate disamenities, such as pests and odours, that may arise from open refuse collection and improve the livability of residents in the direct vicinity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand that DPWCS has been implemented in new towns, such as Bidadari and Tampines North.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The proposed amendments will facilitate its implementation in areas with private developments, such as the future Kampong Bugis area.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What has been the experience of other cities using DPWCS in terms of the cost effectiveness and lifecycle of the system?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What contingencies would be put in place should the DPWCS fail to operate for whatever technical reasons?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such problems, if faced in private developments, can be costly to rectify and may place a huge financial burden on the MCST.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What support could the Government provide to ensure the DPWCS in private developments can be sustainably managed in the long run?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Many resident cleaners usually do not get to enjoy annual salary bonuses because in the Employment Act, the payment of the Annual Wage Supplement, also known as the 13th month bonus, is not mandatory.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the end of each year, the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) U Care Centre receives many enquiries from resident cleaners who asked why they do not receive any bonuses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such guarantees are not present in other jobs for this group of workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, notwithstanding my concerns on DPWCS, these amendments are steps in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And we must continue our tripartite efforts to engage the Government, businesses and workers to create an industry that is ready to tackle the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As Members know, PWM, developed by the tripartite committees, took effect beginning 2015 with the aim of uplifting low-wage workers in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In these sectors, wages had stagnated due to widespread cheap sourcing and due to the more limited scope for collective bargaining, as prices are locked in once service contracts are signed, which are typically for the long term.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The PWM aims to secure for the workers a minimum starting wage and also increases in future wages in line with training and improvements in productivity and standards.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Cleaners, like many other low-wage workers, often live from pay cheque to pay cheque and find it difficult to save for the future.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Today's Bill takes a step in the direction towards minimum wage protection for low-wage workers in the cleaning sector, consistent with helping businesses better attract and retain their workers.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The fact that we are passing today enhancements to the PWM in the cleaning sector offers some cause for optimism that the wage model is taking root in the sector, it is adapting and growing and making progress.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And there, it has grown its own variant of a two-track-roadmap for the provision of more senior workers, as a supervisor or as a specialist technician.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed amendments will help to make a significant difference in the lives of our cleaners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our cleaners play a vital role in our community, and yet some receive very little appreciation for the work they do for us and, for some, they receive very little income as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is a positive step forward and helps to ensure that our cleaners' work becomes a little bit easier and they also feel more appreciated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I worked with our cleaners in Nee Soon East and will share some of their stories in this speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will also make some suggestions on how we can help our cleaners further and seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is an encouraging step to move towards using cleaner and more efficient processes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it will be the Town Council who will maintain it and our maintenance costs might go up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, since the introduction of PWM in 2012, companies across industries have gradually rolled out the changes to positively benefit low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support the proposed move of this Bill to take the PWM a step further by mandating the payment of an Annual Bonus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my interactions with Nee Soon East residents who are cleaners, they have expressed appreciation of this change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Where market forces place a downward pressure on wages of certain sectors, like cleaning, it is important for the Government to intervene.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PWM and now the Annual Bonus are a step in the right direction and help to lift the income levels of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do have some questions and clarifications about the enforcement of PWM.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How are employers who game the system in order to skirt wage increments flagged out?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the penalties or other enforcement mechanisms in place to put pressures on companies to implement recommendations and adhere to the PWM?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State also clarify whether the wages and benefits under the PWM are reset for those who perform the same job functions and roles when the cleaning service providers are changed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the issue now is that it does not apply to all cleaners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the same cleaner is employed by a licensed cleaning company and is sent to the same F&B establishment and does the same exact work as a cleaner, PWM then becomes mandatory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that it might not be easy for us to legislate that PWM is mandatory for all local cleaners regardless of who hires them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But can the Senior Minister of State clarify what MEWR is doing to plug this gap?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is important for cleaners like Ah Eng whom I had the privilege of working with when I gained some experience as a coffee shop cleaner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has been a cleaner for the past two decades and, as I shared on Facebook, "She was so hardworking, so caring and so dedicated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She taught me a lot and a lot more than cleaning a coffee shop." Ah Eng's husband passed away when her two children were still young and she single-handedly brought them up through working as a cleaner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hers is a story of resilience, sacrifice and hard work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that she is currently hired directly by the coffee shop and, as such, PWM is not mandatory for her and she may not receive the Annual Bonus proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I honestly think this is not fair and I sincerely hope that the Senior Minister of State can look into this and ensure that local cleaners like Ah Eng can benefit from the PWM as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our foreign cleaners also do not benefit from PWM.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am grateful that MEWR has encouraged employers to incorporate the principles of progressive wages into the wage structure of their foreign cleaners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If such data is not currently collected, would the Ministry consider collecting this information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PWM is also about increasing productivity and standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM states that, "higher productivity increases business profits for employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Service buyers also enjoy better service standards and quality." But if we leave out our foreign cleaners from the PWM and, bearing in mind that they likely form the bulk of the cleaning sector and workforce, how then will we achieve higher productivity, improve profits and enjoy better service standards and quality?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask if MEWR is looking into this and how to further encourage companies to adopt progressive wage principles for foreign cleaners?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also suggest that MEWR studies what is being done in the construction sector and see if we can implement similar policies for the cleaning sector?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the construction sector, the Higher-skilled (R1) scheme encourages employers to help their workers upskill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This increases the quality and productivity of the workforce and provides wage progression pathways for higher skilled Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MEWR consider this for the cleaning industry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I worked with Hanif who is from Bangladesh and has been a cleaner for the last 12 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I learnt a lot from him, how difficult his life has been and yet how he is so full of smiles and so dedicated about making sure he does his job well for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His enthusiasm for life was infectious and residents love him and treat him not as their cleaner but as their good friend and, for some, their family member.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had dinner with Hanif's family when I was in Bangladesh earlier this year and I saw firsthand how proud they were of him and most of all, how much they miss him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like all of us, Hanif works hard and sacrifices for his family.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hanif got married recently and his wife is now expecting their first child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How difficult it must be to not be with his wife who is now pregnant and how difficult it must be to not be there for his or her childhood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They help to ensure we have a clean environment to live in, to work in and a clean environment to enjoy our food and drinks in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are sometimes a forgotten group of people, and we need to make sure they are fairly treated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am thankful that this Bill highlights the important work they do for all of us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It recognises their efforts and shows how much we appreciate all that they do for us.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, clause 5 of this Bill proposes to add a new Part IIIA to the EPHA, to make it mandatory for designated areas to install and use PWCS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PWCS has the potential of improving the efficiency and standard of waste disposal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if successful, this would reduce the need for manpower in waste management and provide a cleaner living environment for all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The new Part IIIA will enable the Government to designate areas for the implementation of DPWCS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have three queries to raise about this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the status of DPWCS vis-à-vis HDB blocks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, Town Councils manage the common areas in HDB estates, which would include bin chutes and parts of the waste disposal system serving HDB blocks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to a Parliamentary answer given in September 2016, HDB has implemented the PWCS in selected new HDB developments where feasible, including Tampines North, Punggol, Bidadari and Sengkang.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) also said that HDB was studying the feasibility of implementing PWCS in other new housing estates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further stated that for existing estates, HDB would have to assess the outcome of a pilot run in HDB blocks in Yuhua, before deciding whether to roll out the PWCS in other existing estates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a related note, is it the case that PWCS will not be made mandatory for HDB estates?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a difference in the treatment of new blocks?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And is it the case that old blocks will not be required to be retrofitted for PWCS?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second query is how DPWCS areas will be designated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would like the Senior Minister of State to clarify whether the selection of the district is on an ad hoc basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there any criteria used to select the areas for DPWCS and is there a systematic plan to cover all areas in Singapore eventually?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I am concerned about the cost implication of DPWCS for home owners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is quite clear that owners of premises will have to incur significant costs to make their properties PWCS-ready.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The proposed section 31L will empower the Director-General of Public Health to impose requirements on home owners to retrofit existing building infrastructure, maintain and operate certain internal assets, to connect these up to refuse pipeline networks and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The proposed sections 31M and 31N refer to new connection charges and tariff charges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How much of a burden will this impose on smaller condominiums which do not enjoy economies of scale?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of condominiums, there may be particular difficulties if strata-titled owners do not agree to contribute more monies to fund the retrofitting and other costs required, for example, if there is an impending en bloc sale.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the Government handle such a situation?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I think the benefits are tremendous, as mentioned by quite a number of Members.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: On top of it, we can also hope that it helps to reduce infestation of pests, reduce carbon emission and even, in future, help with separation of wastes for recycling.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State clarify, with regard to the implementation of this system, taking into consideration the high capital cost balanced with the manpower and truck cost savings?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: What is the average payback period for implementing such a system at district level?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: What will be the downtime plan in the event of prolonged pipe blockage or other system failures?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, what types of wastes cannot be handled by this system, for example, hazardous chemicals, or residents throwing spongy items that may block the pipes, and how is the Ministry intending to educate the public on this?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my request for clarification, I am in support of this Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially so in a densely populated city state like Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many young Singaporeans take our clean and green environment for granted for they have not been through the days when viruses could spread by indiscriminate spitting, when the river stank of manure, when you could not walk a foot without encountering rubbish or dog poop.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A lot of hard work goes into achieving our current state of affairs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is heartening to note through the amendments to the EPHA that the Government has been reviewing and exploring new ways to manage our waste.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While many housing estates already enjoy a functional and fairly effective waste management system, the area around the bin centre is still a place we do not consider to be pleasant due to the stench and the pests lurking around the area.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the new DPWCS, this problem will, I hope, be eliminated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And with this system, we also reduce our dependence on foreign manpower to move the refuse and drive the refuse trucks, amongst others.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to more efficient waste management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, we should not rest on our laurels when it comes to cultivating good habits of not littering.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At this point in time, technology is not sufficiently extensive to replace work done by humans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The cleaners in my Nee Soon South estates conduct their cleaning three times a day, yet residents are still complaining about the cleanliness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the cleaning of many public areas is done before 6.00 am, and many residents do not realise that because they would not have left home at that time of the day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And, throughout the day, residents and visitors continue to litter or leave their bags of rubbish in public places, which leads to the misconception that the Town Councils are not adequately managing the cleanliness of the estate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can hire many cleaners and we can deploy more technology for quick solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But ultimately, there are many more residents than cleaners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, if residents do not do their part to keep the place clean, the estate will never be as spick and span as they wish it to be.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even a small group of inconsiderate residents is enough to make the estate perpetually dirty.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If one day, the technology breaks down or foreign workers are not available, I shudder at the thought that we will become one big rubbish dump for that day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is crucial to drive home the possibility of this unpleasant scenario to Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, I do litter-picking with residents once a month.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We take turns to do litter-picking at different zones.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will stop cleaning for 24 hours before litter-picking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are also the constituency that started the No Cleaners Day in 2013.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is to enable residents to experience how much rubbish there is when there are no cleaners available and how difficult it is for cleaners to keep the place clean.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Through such exercises, I hope to create awareness and motivate residents to inculcate good habits of not littering.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Naturally, this applies not just in residential blocks, but also in places where people congregate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Often, in open spaces and parks on weekends especially, we see lots of plastic bags and leftover food.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am aware that in some places, extra bins, and sometimes manpower, are deployed to handle the increased amount of rubbish.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, are there more cost-effective and long-term solutions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I applaud the Government for leading by example to reward cleaners for their laborious work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Paying our cleaners higher salary and bonus, of course, is a welcome move.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I think what is more important is to respect them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some residents think that just because they have paid the Town Council service and conservancy charges, the cleaners will have to clean up their mess after they have enjoyed a round of drinks with their friends at the void deck.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They just leave the place and then leave behind beer bottles, peanut skins and so on and expect the cleaners to clean up the mess.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can also lighten the workload of our cleaners, for example, in our office.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After a meeting, we can help to clean the used cups or the litter on the table.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, we can do more and we ought to do more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the cost be passed on to the residents?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that the cleaning companies must now pay bonus to our resident cleaners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, paying our cleaners higher salary and bonus is a welcome move, because their work is not easy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But what is more important is to respect them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is not right that just because you have paid service and conservancy charges, you can do whatever you want, such as leaving beer bottles and peanut shells behind for cleaners to clean up after eating and drinking with friends at the void deck.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is very disrespectful to our cleaners and should be frowned upon.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can also help lighten the workload of the cleaners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The annual bonus for Singaporean and PR cleaners is greatly welcomed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can certainly see the changes brought about by technological advances and automation in the cleaning sector, as in many other sectors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These new machineries and systems will make our cleaners' work less demanding physically.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our cleaners will have to learn new skills to operate these systems and such specific skillsets are expected to lead to higher productivity and wages.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is for our resident cleaners who are elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While they would certainly like to be more productive and earn higher wages, due to their age, they are understandably worried about their abilities to absorb new information and training.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many candidly shared with me that they feel intimidated and fearful, especially those who had little formal education.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They lack the confidence to undergo upgrading of their skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we examine the statistics, we can see that more and more of our elderly are staying in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reason for these queries is to obtain a clearer picture of the manpower profile in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would an employer or contracting company determine productivity when assessing a resident and foreign cleaner doing the same job?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the training be the same for an elderly and a much younger cleaner?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would a trainer deal with language issues in the process of communicating, considering that many elderly cleaners are more proficient in their mother tongue and dialects?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the ability to read and understand instructions and labels, usually in English, have an impact on the future work of our cleaners?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Next, I urge the Government to take a more proactive role to engage our elderly cleaners and understand their concerns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the dialogues with them, please use the feedback to improve training programmes, customising them if necessary.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such interactions also provide opportunities for our Government agencies to encourage them to embrace skills upgrading, so that psychological barriers will be lowered and they will be more receptive to training and new ways of doing their jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English) Finally, I also appeal to the Ministry to ensure that our cleaners do not continue to be disadvantaged by the subcontracting culture in the cleaning sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such common practices may depress the wages of our cleaners and fail to recognise their experience and higher skillsets as clients go through a merry-go-round of cleaning contracting companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On DPWCS, the benefits of it are plain to appreciate, and the hon Senior Minister of State has enumerated them in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I would also add that this system would go a long way in helping our Government achieve its stated intent of reaching 70% recycling rate by 2030.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Member Ms Irene Quay just mentioned, this is because the DPWCS supports separation of waste.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also follows the example in a number of other countries, as mentioned by the learned Senior Minister of State, such as Sweden, South Korea and the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, as mentioned by the learned Senior Minister of State, there was an HDB pilot run in several locations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be standards ascribed for the licensees to follow via subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, gleaning from the experience of other countries, a point that hon Member Mr Zainal Sapari made, will there also be quality of service standards in terms of effecting recovery?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it be lower compared to the current system?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I gather from the HDB pilot that there was an MND grant provided to the Town Council to deal with extra costs associated with the implementation of the pilot.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What would be the expected costs for the residents?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be regulation or guidance given to licensees on how the tariffs should be implemented for residents?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the proposed section 31F excludes premises controlled or managed by a Town Council, a point highlighted by hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should NEA not be the agency to regulate all DPWCSs in housing estates, public or private, just like the regulation of water pipes?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does NEA also contemplate having a DPWCS that serves both public and private estates, such that residents can enjoy a higher level of scale and potentially higher cost savings as well?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can NEA consider something similar to the HDB pilots like, for example, MND grants?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I move on to the introduction of the PWM Bonus.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I fully support the amendments which adopt the recommendation of the TCC chaired by the hon Member Mr Zainal Sapari.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment directly helps these cleaners better cope with cost-of-living issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am concerned, however, about the impact vis-a-vis existing cleaning contracts with margins already locked in, a point that Mr Chen Show Mao highlighted just now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that under the proposed section 80H(6) of the Bill, the Director-General will have the power to postpone the effective date of specified amount by the Commissioner for Labour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What would be the considerations the Director-General have in mind before exercising this power?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How would he strike the balance between ensuring that the cleaners benefit from these wage increases on one hand, and also deal with the predicament of cleaning contractors who are already locked in on the price of cleaning contracts, which still have a significant performance period to perform?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The implementation of DPWCS is a great step towards greater efficiency and a higher standard of hygiene in the treatment of our refuse collection.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will boost productivity of our cleaning system substantially.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially important in view of the difficulties we face in attracting and retaining workers in this sector and our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The pneumatic system will reduce smell and exposure to pests, such as rats and cockroaches, which are common in open refuse collection systems.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to note that the amendments will provide for the implementation of PWCS on a larger scale and bring more residences under the system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What I would like to raise for the attention of the Ministry is the maintenance and repair issues for this more complex system of refuse collection.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures are in place to enable vendors to detect faulty mechanics in the system which can ultimately lead to malfunction?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had encountered an isolated mechanical fault which caused the breakdown of the compactor, leading to the failure of discharge of waste at one of the rubbish chutes in my constituency early this year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The compactor broke down without the awareness of the collector.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are the workers adequately trained to recognise signs of trouble, especially if it is hidden within the system, so that they can alert the maintenance and repair team as soon as possible?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once the system or mechanics break down, what are the contingency plans to ensure refuse continues to be collected and removed to prevent hygiene problems?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the new regulations to build PWCS in more areas in our country.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: PWCS uses pneumatics to transport refuse to a central collection centre through pipes, greatly reducing the reliance on manpower, and also reduce foul odours and cockroaches and rats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am worried that there are some bad apples among residents who throw oversized items into the refuse chutes, causing blockages, leading to system failure.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry would put more effort into public education to teach residents how to use this new system in the correct way to ensure its smooth operation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a way for the system to retrieve valuables accidentally thrown away within a short time?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The cleaning sector is an important and indispensable part of our economy, not only in its contribution to our environmental hygiene and disease prevention, but also in maintaining our infrastructure and facilities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: ES enables other sectors and industries to function smoothly and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a particularly labour-intensive sector, which is worrying for us as we face manpower shortages amidst an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, as more and more of our younger generation receive higher education and the variety of jobs open to them increases, there might be fewer who are willing to take on traditional cleaning sector jobs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fortunately, technology will play an increasingly bigger role in ES.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Automation will help to boost productivity and take over an increasing number of the less pleasant chores.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It does away with manual refuse haulage altogether – an essential but laborious, repetitive and unpleasant task – and substantially reduce the disamenities, such as foul odours and pests.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, just as we need to continue to educate and remind our residents that nothing except human waste and toilet paper should be flushed down the toilet, we have to teach residents what should and should not be thrown into refuse hoppers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who may not be aware, "fatbergs" are formed by things which should not be thrown into toilets like plasters, sanitary towels, nappies, condoms, all of these things that we have always been told not to do; it can lead to things like this.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This public education exercise has to be held in conjunction with recycling initiatives and also the provision of conveniently located disposal areas for bulky items.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the adoption of progressive wage practices in the cleaning industry will lead to more stability in employment, and also continuous skills upgrading and greater productivity.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In tandem with technological advances and innovation in the cleaning industry, cleaning will evolve as a profession.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Specific skills will be needed to operate more complex machinery and systems and the remuneration will adjust up accordingly.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, in future, autonomous vehicles will be used to clean buildings and streets.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our cleaners’ jobs will then be running these fleets of cleaning bots, which require very different skillsets.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I appeal to the Government to implement and enforce more stringent measures to protect our workers in the cleaning sector.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They face many risky situations and hazardous materials in the course of their work, including chemicals they have to work with, physical hazards, and micro-organisms, such as viruses, bacteria and moulds.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers and contractors must be held accountable for measures to protect our cleaners' health and safety.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should also monitor their workloads and schedules to prevent exploitation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By improving the treatment and work conditions of our cleaners, companies will benefit from retaining and attracting experienced and better qualified staff, who will contribute to higher productivity and quality services for clients.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through vigorous tripartite efforts, and especially by the hon Member of Parliament Mr Lim Swee Say and relentless, passionate advocacy of my fellow unionist Mr Zainal Sapari, we had reversed the downward spiral of decreasing wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is now a ladder that the 46,000 cleaners can work towards higher wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can add on and strengthen this ladder today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would this result in a near-term increase in the cost of cleaning?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But it would also spur our companies to look into suitable technologies to help our cleaners do their work better and it also promotes greater retention for workers to scale the ladder over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must be under no delusion that this ladder is neither a panacea nor a foolproof way of raising our cleaners' wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, our work is not anywhere near done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This ladder and PWM Bonus can be defeated or circumvented.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, when service buyers ask for prices without the accompanying technological improvements, then it must necessarily mean that workers must now perform more duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Coupled with the competitive cleaning landscape, workers might end up doing a lot more than expected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry ensure that our workers are not disadvantaged inadvertently as a result of this Bonus?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of the cleaners are also older and less educated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can help to weed out unscrupulous employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, we can better protect the interests of the workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the implementation details are being developed, I hope that the Ministry can prevent companies from putting in onerous work demands for cleaners to qualify for the PWM Bonus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, some companies might attach attendance and medical certificate records as prequalifiers for the PWM Bonus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many writers, observers and residents have often lamented that the cleaners' work is difficult but the wages are low.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even with this PWM Bonus, we would still like for their wages to improve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The consumers and, hence, the market, does not place a high value on cleaning services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a consequent commoditisation of cleaning services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, when service buyers consume such cleaning services, they often look for the cheapest contract.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, they hope that they can be cheaper with every contract renewal.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While there is, indeed, room for productivity gains, much of the cleaners' work has a productivity limit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, there is limited foreseeable technology to help a cleaner clear the table faster.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, our lamentations must be consistent with our consumption patterns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As Member of Parliament Zainal Sapari elegantly stated, "You can outsource your services, but you cannot outsource your responsibilities." Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, since we introduced PWM, we have successfully reversed the downward spiral of our cleaners' wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through the efforts of the tripartite partners, former Minister Lim Swee Say and my fellow NTUC colleague Mr Zainal Sapari, a solid foundation has been laid for our cleaners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Upon this very strong foundation, we can continue to seek more benefits for our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The mandatory PWM Bonus can further increase the wage of our workers and promote fairer sharing of profits between employers and their workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Although there might be sporadic cost increases, it will spur employers to adopt technology to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We, as consumers, also have the responsibility to ensure that outsourced cleaning contracts must stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Not only do we want value for money but also treat our cleaners fairly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the way ahead is one where we must continue to build on the efforts of the Tripartite Committee on Cleaning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must strengthen PWM and not undermine it with our consumption habits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The PWM Bonus is a step in the right direction in helping our workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I generally support the amendments proposed, there are two areas within the Bill that I would like to speak on.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first pertains to clause 4 to amend section 17 of the Act.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Littering in public places remains a concern, despite us having sufficient rubbish bins in and around Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are those who choose to throw their refuse near or just next to a rubbish bin instead of into it, something that many of us, as grassroots advisers or Town Councillors, have observed or received residents’ feedback on.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that it remains prohibited to “throw litter in a receptacle not provided for the deposit of refuse and rubbish”.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I support the amendments to section 17 to further specify the prohibition against throwing refuse in any public place.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are make-shift rubbish bins which good Samaritans and individuals create to collect rubbish during community events or private functions, such as a makeshift rubbish bin made using cardboard boxes or pails lined with plastic bags.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would also like to urge the Ministry to do more to clamp down on errant litterbugs, particularly high-rise litterbugs, who have no qualms about throwing both big and small items out of their flat windows, as well as motorists who throw their cigarette butts willfully out of their vehicle windows or from their motorcycles onto the road or central road dividers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have raised the latter in an earlier Parliamentary Question in March this year and I recognise the difficulty in enforcing littering fines on such errant litterbugs as the action is fleeting and the litterbug is usually on the move while on the roads, hence difficult to capture on video camera, for instance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not a small number, and inconsiderate acts leading to such fires should be clamped on decisively.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, for driving or riding safety, these motorists should not be holding a lighted cigarette anyway.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should always have both their hands on the steering wheel or handlebar at all times.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is too short a time to catch the litterbug in action.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents consistently share such acts of high-rise littering happening in our housing estates.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just last week, while looking out the window of my third floor flat, I saw a medium-sized plastic bag falling right in front of my eyes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It seems that high-rise litterbugs are undeterred, despite NEA’s enforcement and our public education efforts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I support the introduction of the PWM for Cleaners, I would like to ask the Ministry how do we define work performance?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, Town Council cleaners sweep the floor of our housing estates every day but there are inconsiderate individuals, residents or otherwise, who litter, be it late at night or in the wee hours of the morning.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we expect the cleaners to keep up with cleaning the housing estate at all hours of the day 24/7?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It cannot be the case where just because we find some litter in the estate it means that the cleaners have not done their work properly.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The onus is on each and every one of us to keep our housing estates clean by not littering and by throwing our rubbish in appropriate places, such as waste bins and rubbish chutes, as well as cleaning up after ourselves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned if the inconsiderate acts of others will inadvertently have a significantly negative effect on the income of our cleaners, especially in terms of income related to their work performance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They have also raised many thoughtful comments, which I will now address.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how connection charges and tariffs will be determined and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked if residents would have to foot these costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In Kampong Bugis, NEA will collect this from the Master Developer.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The connection charge will be small compared to other costs like land costs and construction costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, it will be a very small proportion.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will be made known to bidders when the site is launched for sale so that this would be factored in their bids.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will cover operational and maintenance expenses for DPWCS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The MCSTs will then collect payments towards this tariff from subsidiary proprietors under the MCST as part of their monthly maintenance fees.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To keep overall costs competitive, NEA will appoint the DPWCS licensee for Kampong Bugis through an open tender.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The tariffs will take into account factors, such as gross floor area (GFA) and amount of refuse generated for the different types of premises.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, for example, the tariffs for residential premises will be different from that for commercial premises.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Irene Quay, Mr Zainal Sapari and Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about potential cost increases arising from DPWCS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will make every effort to ensure that the costs of waste collection remain affordable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But we also have to balance short-term costs with long-term sustainability.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
